Oregon Court of Appeals: The smell of cannabis smoke is not objectively unpleasant.

TL;DR: Guy calls the cops because his neighbor's weed smoke was drifting into his home. Cops got a warrant to search the smoker's home for evidence of "disorderly conduct" (creating a hazardous or physically offensive condition), found evidence that he had been spraying graffiti and he was then charged and convicted of criminal mischief.

Appeals court rules the search was illegal because while some smells (such as sewage or rotten eggs) are objectively unpleasant, marijuana smoke is not.

Depression is a symptom. Generally, when neurons are in distress, you see it. Sometimes the neurotransmitter activity that marks depression is caused by something else in the body, like unhappy microbes in the guy (they make a lot of neurotransmitters). Ultimately, the causes are various.

This is why research is all over the place on the subject.

You can treat a symptom, with meds or therapy - exercise works best - but if you don't find and address the underlying problem, it's not going to go away unless your body is able to recover on its own.

Evolutionary purpose? Depressed people have a lower desire to be active so they are more likely to ignore other stimuli and give themselves time to recover. It also gives them time to reflect on what the cause might be (bad food, bad social environment, &c).

Depression is a valuable symptom of winter and hibernation. Keeps you indoors and safe and lowers your metabolism. Saves up energy for spring. A new mother will get it to establish strong emotional bonds with the newborn and gives time for body to prepare for the next baby.

Severe depression can cause anger and dislike which will force changes in situations or environment.

Up and down go hand in hand.

Crops have an up and down cycle as many things in nature - wild fires, floods, volcanoes. Ask Spielberg if you can be happy without sad.

Depression's Evolutionary Roots

I enjoy your argument, but your premise about humans evolving to be overly optimistic, encouraging risk-taking, is in fact incorrect.

Loss aversion bias plays a large role in the 'average' human, and in theory this is due to the fact that incorrectly taking a risk (trying to take down a gazelle in lion territory and getting killed) is worse than incorrectly being cautious (you simply eat something smaller for the day and evaluate tomorrow's risks tomorrow). Although I'm a bit lazy to go into details on everything, the wikipedia article seems to have some nice sources.

With all that said, depression has shown an increase in the ability to go into depth with introspection, which may be good if there's some problems in your life, and you need to take the time to figure them out before moving on. It also influences self-perception, and in actuality, people who are depressed self-report more accurately in regards to their virtues/flaws. Theoretically, this could implicate a higher ability to pinpoint some cognitive or behavioral blemishes that could be adjusted to make you a better person.

Finally, unless I'm mistaken, I believe people who are depressed show higher levels of empathic concern within situations in which they feel distressed (ie. they would be more likely to console someone who is upset because it upsets them to see someone upset). Evolutionarily, this could be beneficial because people tend to appreciate and remember those who are kind to them in times of need, magnitudes more than when they're already happy. Group selection and all.

I enjoy your argument, but your premise about humans evolving to be overly optimistic, encouraging risk-taking, is in fact incorrect.
